newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - French election, US payrolls dominate.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - French election, US payrolls dominate.

text.p: The twin concerns of European currency union and U.S. interest rates will continue to rumble through financial markets in the week ahead, analysts said on Friday.

French elections and U.S. payroll data will top the bill as volatile markets struggle to make sense of both issues. A Canadian election and British monetary policy will also feature, along with French and German GDP data.
"It's going to be a particularly volatile week between now and next Friday," Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International here, said.
"Not only have we got the French elections to negotiate, we've got the Canadian federal election on Monday and key May activity data in the U.S.," he said.

Analysts said victory by left-wing parties in the second round of French elections on Sunday was fairly well discounted in French markets but would nevertheless continue to fuel concerns about European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Meanwhile the row between the German government and the Bundesbank over the revaluation of gold assets to qualify for a single currency will stay under the spotlight next week.

Markets would likely continue to price in a wider and softer euro, sending German yields higher towards yields of peripheral bonds -- turning convergence upside down -- and the mark weaker against the dollar, analysts said.

"It's probably going to be translated as increased likelihood of a broad-based start to EMU and additional fudging of the criteria," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist Europe at BankAmerica. "It ought to cement a fairly soft end of the Deutschemark against the dollar."
Beyond the French election, U.S. data would be poured over for any inkling of interest rate policy before the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting (FOMC) on July 1-2.

The May report from the National Association of Purchasing Management starts the rush on Monday, followed by April leading indicators on Tuesday, April factory orders on Wednesday and ending with the clincher on Friday -- May payrolls.
"My view is the U.S. economy is doing rather well," Peter Osler, head of research at GNI in London. "The data we are going to get is going to point to an FOMC move on July 1," he said.
Canadian parliamentary elections on Monday will likely be far less troublesome for financial markets than the French election, analysts said.
Canada's Liberal party was poised to return to government with its majority intact and will face a Reform opposition, a poll published on Friday by Toronto's Globe and Mail newspaper showed.

The poll showed support for the Liberals at 39 percent, compared with 20 percent for the Conservatives, 19 percent for the right-wing Reform Party and only 9.0 percent for the separatist Bloc Quebecois.
Such a result would oust the Bloc from official opposition and could quell the separatist movement in Quebec.

In Europe, Britain has a scattering of economic data, including provisional May M0 money supply, final April M4 and the May Purchasing Managers Index on Monday. The Confederation of British Industry's releases its distributive trades survey for May on Thursday.
"The Purchasing Managers Survey will show strength of domestic demand and weakness on the exports side," Osler said.

On Monday, Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will announce the date of his first budget, according to a government source, while the new-style Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meets on Thursday and Friday.
UK markets will be waiting news of who is to sit on the new nine-person committee as Brown is yet to choose his four appointees.
"If they haven't got the whole council together it might look a little gung-ho to move on rates and so although it's quite a close call I'd say on balance they would leave it," Osler said.
Additional data included German Q1 GDP, French April unemployment and German April industrial production and manufacturing new orders. --International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
